ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

Pictured: Cranium 17 of the Sima de los Huesos, from an individual from the same location and time period. Nohemi Sala, Juan Luis Arsuaga, Ana Pantoja-Pérez, Adrián Pablos, Ignacio Martínez, Rolf M. Quam, Asier Gómez-Olivencia, José María Bermúdez de Castro, Eudald Carbonell, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Bishop Teodomiro
famous.story_individual:
Bishop Teodomiro of Iria Flavia was an important figure in the history of Christian pilgrimage in medieval Spain. Born in the late 8th century, likely in the region of Galicia, Teodomiro rose to prominence within the Church, becoming the Bishop of Iria Flavia around 819 AD.

Teodomiro's most significant claim to fame came between 820 and 830 AD when, according to tradition, he discovered the tomb of St James the Apostle. The legend states that Teodomiro, guided by divine revelation and following directions from a local hermit, located the remains of St James in an abandoned cemetery in what is now Santiago de Compostela.

Bishop Teodomiro and angel during the legendary discovery of the tomb of St James. Tumbo A of the Cathedral of Santiago, Public Domain, via The Scholarly Pilgrim.

This discovery transformed the region. Upon hearing the news, King Alfonso II of Asturias traveled to the site, establishing the first pilgrimage route known as the Camino Primitivo. Teodomiro's find catapulted Santiago de Compostela into prominence as one of Christianity's major pilgrimage destinations, rivaling Rome and Jerusalem.

Throughout his tenure as bishop, Teodomiro likely played a crucial role in the early development of the following of St. James and the establishment of Santiago de Compostela as a religious center. He died on October 20, 847 AD, as recorded on his tombstone, discovered in 1955 beneath the floor of Santiago Cathedral.

The tombstone or lid of the sarcophagus of Bishop Teodomiro of Iria Flavia was discovered by Chamoso Lamas in 1955. The inscription on it reads: IN HOC TVMVLO REQVIESCIT FAMULUS DI THEODEMIRVS HIRIENSE SEDIS EPS QVI OBIIT XIII KLDS NBRS ERA DCCCLXXXV (In this tomb rests the servant of God Teodomiro, Bishop of the See of Iria, who died on the 13th of the Kalends of November in the year 885) (© Fundación Catedral de Santiago). Fig. 2 from Pérez-Ramallo et al. 2024.

Scientific analyses of remains associated with Teodomiro's tomb suggest he was an older man at the time of his death, possibly with mixed ancestral origins reflecting the complex demographic interactions of the Iberian Peninsula during the early medieval period. These studies have provided new insights into the life of this influential religious figure, whose actions shaped the spiritual landscape of medieval Europe.

References

  • Pérez-Ramallo P, Rodríguez-Varela R, Staniewska A, et al. Unveiling Bishop Teodomiro of Iria Flavia? An attempt to identify the discoverer of St James’s tomb through osteological and biomolecular analyses (Santiago de Compostela, Galicia, Spain). Antiquity. Published online 2024:1-18. doi:10.15184/aqy.2024.91

famous.name: Birka Viking Warrior Woman
famous.story_individual:
In the early-to-mid 10th century, a high-ranking female warrior was laid to rest in an elaborate chamber grave near the garrison of Birka, Sweden. She died in her 30s or older, based on analysis of her bones. She was dressed in fine silk clothing with silver thread decorations, indicating her elite status in Viking society.

Sketch of archaeological grave found and labeled "Bj581" by Hjalmar Stolpe in Birka, Sweden. Published 1889. Evalo Hansen, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

DNA analysis shows she was genetically similar to present-day British Isles, North Atlantic Islands, and Scandinavia populations. Strontium isotope analysis of her teeth suggests she was not born in Birka but moved there sometime in her early years, reflecting the mobility of Viking Age elites.

As a warrior, she was equipped with a complete set of professional weapons: a sword, axe, spear, battle knife, and armor-piercing arrows. The presence of two horses - a mare and a stallion - in her grave further emphasized her high status. She appears to have been not just a warrior but a military leader, as suggested by the gaming pieces and board found with her that indicate knowledge of tactical strategy.

Her burial location was significant - marked by a large stone boulder on an elevated terrace adjacent to Birka's garrison. She was interred at a time when Birka was a thriving trade center, connecting Scandinavian networks to places as distant as the Arab world and China.

This remarkable woman challenges our understanding of Viking Age gender roles, suggesting that some women could attain high-ranking military positions in what was traditionally viewed as a male-dominated sphere. The presence of an Arab silver dirham from the reign of al-Muktadir in her grave helps archaeologists place her burial firmly within the early 10th century when Birka stood at the crossroads of far-reaching trade networks.

References

  • Hedenstierna-Jonson, C., Kjellström, A., Zachrisson, T., Krzewińska, M., Sobrado, V., Price, N., Günther, T., Jakobsson, M., Götherström, A., & Storå, J. (2017). A female Viking warrior confirmed by genomics. American Journal of Physical Anthropology, 164(4), 853-860. https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.23308

  • Price, N., Hedenstierna-Jonson, C., Zachrisson, T., Kjellström, A., Storå, J., Krzewińska, M., … Götherström, A. (2019). Viking warrior women? Reassessing Birka chamber grave Bj.581. Antiquity, 93(367), 181–198. doi:10.15184/aqy.2018.258

famous.name: Virginia Eriksdotter
famous.story_individual:
Virginia Eriksdotter was the illegitimate daughter of King Erik XIV of Sweden and his royal mistress Agda Persdotter. Her mother, known as "Agda i Porten" (Agda of the Gate), served as the official royal mistress to Crown Prince Erik during 1558-1561 and had her own apartments at Kalmar Castle, where Virginia was born.

In 1561, Virginia and her sister Constantia were forcibly removed from their mother's custody—violating Swedish law—and placed under the care of Princess Cecilia and later Princess Elizabeth of Sweden. In 1566, King Erik XIV proposed Virginia's marriage to Tsarevich Ivan Ivanovich of Russia, which she refused. During the Sture Murders of 1567, she was approached to intercede with the king on behalf of imprisoned nobles.

After her father's deposition in 1568, Virginia maintained her position in society, receiving estates from both King John III and Charles IX. In 1586, she married nobleman Håkan Knutsson Hand, governor of Kronoberg Castle, and had seven children.

Her detailed mitochondrial haplogroup was determined by mtFull Sequence testing of a descendant and reported in the Sweden DNA Project. The lineage is documented at WikiTree. It has not yet been confirmed by a second test result.

famous.name: Bridgettine Relic B
famous.story_individual:
Skull B is one of two human crania long preserved in an ornate silver-gilt relic shrine at Vadstena Abbey in Östergötland, central Sweden. For centuries, Catholic tradition identified it as the skull of Blessed Katarina, also known as Catherine of Sweden (c. 1331-1381), the daughter of Saint Birgitta (Birgitta Birgersdotter, 1303-1373). Saint Birgitta, a Swedish mystic and visionary whose revelations shaped Church reform efforts, founded the Bridgettine Order and is one of Europe's six patron saints. Katarina accompanied her mother on pilgrimages to Rome and the Holy Land, helped promote the order after Birgitta's death in 1373, and was herself beatified. Her remains were reportedly brought to Vadstena Abbey, the motherhouse of the order, and placed in the shrine in 1489 alongside other relics.

The shrine, housed today in Vadstena's Blue Church (Blå Kyrkan), historically contained two skulls and dozens of additional bones attributed to saints and pious figures. Mid-20th-century anthropological examination tentatively assigned the more gracile, younger-looking Skull B, estimated at about 50-55 years at death, with a compact structure, yellow-brown coloration, good overall preservation, and a single small benign osteoma (bony growth) roughly 8 mm across, to Katarina. The other cranium, Skull A, appeared more robust and was linked to Birgitta.

In the early 2000s, Vadstena parish commissioned a multidisciplinary scientific investigation led by researchers at Uppsala University, including Marie Allen's group. The study combined physical anthropology, ancient DNA analysis, and radiocarbon dating to evaluate authenticity and the claimed mother-daughter relationship. For Skull B, nuclear DNA testing via the Amelogenin gene, along with cranial morphology, confirmed it belonged to a female whose estimated age aligned reasonably with Katarina's lifespan.

Mitochondrial DNA sequencing focused on the hypervariable regions and a few diagnostic coding-region positions. This revealed at least six nucleotide differences from Skull A, more than enough under forensic guidelines to exclude a maternal relationship; the sequences were consistent with unrelated European individuals. A later analysis of the low-coverage data by FamilyTreeDNA assigned Skull B to mitochondrial haplogroup T2, though no further subclade refinement was possible without additional higher-coverage testing.

Radiocarbon dating placed Skull B within the calibrated range of approximately 1470-1670 AD, roughly 89-289 years after Katarina's death in 1381. Stable isotope analysis indicated a mainly terrestrial diet, with possible minor freshwater fish consumption, but this did not significantly affect the date through reservoir effects. In comparison, Skull A likely belongs to haplogroup H according to analysis by FamilyTreeDNA (again without further subclade resolution from the low-coverage data) and is dated even earlier, to 1215-1270 cal AD, which is equally incompatible with Birgitta's timeline.

The combined evidence demonstrates that Skull B cannot be Katarina's remains, nor is it maternally related to Skull A. A third skull, once in the shrine (stolen in 1645), had already been ruled out on morphological grounds. Instead, the collection appears to represent an accumulation of medieval and early modern bones assembled over time as devotional objects for pilgrims and the Bridgettine community, rather than the specific remains of the named saints.

Despite the scientific disconfirmation, Skull B continues to be venerated as a relic in Vadstena. It is presented here because of its historical significance.

Pictured: The putative skull of St. Birgitta (Skull A) to the right and the putative skull of Katarina (Skull B) to the left. Photo: Hans Lundberg. Creative Commons Attribution License.

Reference

  • Nilsson M, Possnert G, Edlund H, Budowle B, Kjellström A, et al. (2010) Analysis of the Putative Remains of a European Patron Saint–St. Birgitta. PLOS ONE 5(2): e8986. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0008986

famous.name: James Lord Pierpont
famous.story_individual:
James Lord Pierpont was an American songwriter, organist, and music teacher, notable as the uncle of financier J.P. Morgan. Making his living through church music and private lessons, he would go on to compose one of America's most beloved holiday songs, though he wouldn't live to see its enormous success.

His most significant achievement came in 1857 with the publication of "The One Horse Open Sleigh" by Oliver Ditson and Company in Boston. The song, which was first performed at Boston's Ordway Hall minstrel theater, was rereleased in 1859 as "Jingle Bells." While the original version wasn't an immediate hit, later arrangements with a simplified chorus melody transformed it into the classic we know today.

Before composing "Jingle Bells," Pierpont lived an adventurous life that included joining the California Gold Rush in the 1850s, where he sought his fortune like many others of his era. Despite coming from a prominent New England family, he chose a more bohemian path than his wealthy relatives, moving frequently and trying his hand at various ventures before finding his place in music. The contrast between his wandering lifestyle and his creation of one of America's most enduring holiday songs makes his legacy particularly intriguing.

His mtDNA haplogroup was determined by mtDNA testing of his matrilineal relative and documented on WikiTree.

famous.name: Tsar Nicholas II Romanov
famous.story_individual:
The last Emperor of Russia, King of Congress Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland, Nicholas II or Nikolai II Alexandrovich Romanov (1868-1918) reigned from November 1, 1894 until his abdication on March 15, 1917. He is known as Saint Nicholas the Passion-Bearer in the Russian Orthodox Church.

Nicholas supported Serbia during the July Crisis and authorized the Russian Army's mobilization on July 30, 1914. In response, Germany declared war on Russia and its ally France, launching the Great War, often known as WWI.

The Russian Provisional Government imprisoned Nicholas and his family and banished them to Siberia as a result of several military defeats and low morale at home and on the battlefield. The family was detained in Yekaterinburg following the Bolsheviks' taking power, and the Romanovs were killed there on July 17, 1918.

The consensus among historians is that Nicholas was a well-intentioned but ineffective leader who proved unable to handle the issues his country faced.

Nicholas was a cousin to Great Britain’s King George V as well as the father of Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna, the inspiration for the 1997 movie Anastasia.

References

  • Rogaev, E. I., Grigorenko, A. P., Moliaka, Y. K., Faskhutdinova, G., Goltsov, A., Lahti, A., Hildebrandt, C., Kittler, E. L., & Morozova, I. (2009). Genomic identification in the historical case of the Nicholas II royal family. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 106(13), 5258-5263. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0811190106

Information sourced from Wikipedia, Biography.com, and Britannica.

famous.name: Gösta Ekman Jr.
famous.story_individual:
Gösta Ekman (junior), born Carl Gösta Ingemar Ekman in 1939, was a distinguished figure in Swedish entertainment, renowned for his contributions to theater, film, and television. His legacy is marked by a versatile career that saw him excel in both comedic and dramatic roles, making him a beloved actor across generations.

Coming from a lineage deeply rooted in the performing arts, with his father, Hasse Ekman, and grandfather, Gösta Ekman (senior), both being eminent personalities in Swedish cinema and theater, Ekman inherited a passion and talent for acting. This background set the stage for a career that would leave a significant mark on the Swedish cultural landscape.

One of Ekman's most celebrated roles was as the lead detective Martin Beck in the Swedish television series, an adaptation of the crime novels by Maj Sjöwall and Per Wahlöö. His portrayal of Beck brought the character to life with depth and nuance, contributing to the international popularity of Swedish crime dramas.

Throughout his career, Ekman received numerous awards and honors, recognizing his profound impact on the arts in Sweden. His work not only entertained but also contributed to the country’s cultural fabric, earning him a place among the most respected figures in Swedish entertainment.

His brother Mikael Ekman directed four of the Jönssonligan films, with Gösta in the lead role. Mikael's mtFull Sequence testing determined their detailed mitochondrial haplogroup, which was reported in the Sweden DNA Project and on WikiTree.

Pictured: Gösta Ekman at Dramaten (2014), Frankie Fouganthin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Biographical information sourced from Wikipedia. Biography in part generated using OpenAI (2024) ChatGPT-4 [Large multimodal model].

famous.name: Ozzy Osbourne
famous.story_individual:
Ozzy Osbourne, born in Birmingham, England, rose to fame as the lead singer of Black Sabbath, helping create heavy metal music and earning the nickname "Prince of Darkness." After leaving Sabbath in 1979, he built a successful solo career marked by both hit albums and notorious incidents, including the infamous bat-biting episode of 1982.

What makes Osbourne particularly fascinating to scientists is his seemingly superhuman resilience through decades of extreme substance abuse and numerous near-fatal accidents. This led to him being selected for groundbreaking genetic research in 2010, when Knome and Cofactor Genomics conducted whole genome sequencing on his DNA. The study took three weeks to complete and revealed several significant findings.

His mitochondrial DNA was identified as belonging to haplogroup T2. The genetic study also revealed several novel variations in how his body processes drugs and alcohol, potentially explaining how he survived years of substance abuse that claimed many of his contemporaries.

Today, while managing Parkinson's disease, Osbourne continues to be celebrated as one of rock music's greatest icons. His influence extends from his groundbreaking work with Black Sabbath to his successful solo career, inspiring generations of musicians. Beyond the stage, his unique genetic makeup has provided valuable insights for scientific research, adding another fascinating chapter to the legend of the Prince of Darkness.

Pictured: Ozzy Osbourne (1973), by Premier, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model].

famous.name: Eddie Izzard
famous.story_individual:
Eddie Izzard is a British stand-up comedian, actor, writer, and political activist known for a whimsical and surreal comedic style. Born in Yemen to British parents, Eddie had an itinerant childhood due to his father's work with British Petroleum. A prominent figure in LGBTQ+ advocacy, Izzard, who identifies as transgender and uses she/her pronouns, has campaigned extensively for the UK's Labour Party and transgender rights.

Her breakthrough in America was the Emmy-winning HBO special "Dress to Kill." Izzard has also starred in films like "Ocean's Twelve" and "Ocean's Thirteen," and the TV series "The Riches." She's recognized for her charity work and for running numerous marathons for causes such as Sport Relief.

Eddie Izzard’s father was Harold John Michael Izzard (1928–2018) and the surname is of French Huguenot origin.

"Meet the Izzards" was a two-part television documentary broadcast on BBC One in February 2013. The show follows Eddie Izzard as she embarks on a journey to trace her genetic history using DNA.

The first part of the documentary, "The Mum's Line," focuses on Eddie's maternal lineage through mitochondrial DNA testing, tracking down distant relatives who share a common ancestor with her mother. This journey takes Eddie from Britain to Denmark and Germany, and back into more distant history. The mtDNA haplogroup was revealed to be T2f1a1.

In the second part, "The Dad's Line," Eddie traces her paternal ancestry through Y chromosome testing, finding connections that stretch from Britain to Scandinavia and further back to Africa, uncovering the path of her ancient ancestors' migration out of Africa about 10,000 generations ago. The broad Y-DNA haplogroup I-M223 was revealed in this episode.

Video: Meet the Izzards (BBC One, February 2012)

famous.name: Collin McKinney
famous.story_individual:
The son of an American Revolutionary War soldier, Collin McKinney spent much of his early life in Virginia, Kentucky, and Tennessee. In 1826, he moved his family to the Red River Colony in Northeast Texas, where his friend Benjamin Milam was recruiting settlers.

One of the “Fearless Fifty-Nine,” McKinney was a delegate to the Convention of 1836 in Washington-on-the-Brazos. He was appointed to draft the Texas Declaration of Independence along with four other men. After the Texas Revolution, he was a member of the committee that drafted the Constitution of the Republic of Texas and was elected to the House of Representatives for the Congress of the Republic of Texas. 

In the 1840s, McKinney made eleven trips on horseback to Kentucky and Tennessee, guiding hundreds of settlers to North Texas. Before his death in 1861, he was a vocal opponent of secession despite being the largest slaveowner in his county.

A significant influence in shaping early Texas history and politics, he is the namesake of Collin County and its county seat, McKinney, Texas. 

Collin McKinney’s Y-DNA and mtDNA haplogroups have been inferred from Big Y and mtFull Sequence testing of descendants as shared on WikiTree.

Biographical information sourced from The Handbook of Texas Online and the University of Texas at Arlington McKinney and Milam Family Papers collection. Pictured: Collin McKinney, Public Domain, via WikiTree.

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.

Homo neanderthalensis reconstruction - Mr. N

©Neanderthal Museum

The divergence time between modern human and Neanderthal Y chromosomes was estimated by Petr et al. 2020. The evolutionary history of Neanderthal and Denisovan Y chromosomes. The A000-T haplogroup name comes from the ISOGG Y-DNA Haplogroup Tree 2019-2020.
